newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS - Danish share index seen continuing climb.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Danish share index seen continuing climb.

text.p: Denmark's KFX top-20 share index, which has set new highs on each of the past six trading days, will climb further in the fourth quarter of 1996 and stand 6.7 percent up by October 1997, analysts said on Tuesday.

With the index around 126 on Tuesday afternoon and expected to close at yet another high, analysts said the stong Danish economy should keep sentiment, and prices, buoyant despite occasional blips as players took profits.
"There are very strong fundamentals, with growth increasing both in Denmark and in the European countries where we sell our exports," BG Bank Head of Research Frank Fryd Petersen said.

The index has gained nine points -- or 13 percent -- in the past three months and a panel of eight analysts, most of whom insisted on anonymity, was generally optimistic, predicting an average 0.8 percent rise over the three months from October 4.
Over the next six months they saw the index rising by 3.8 percent and forecast that it would be 6.7 percent higher by this time next year.

The average was weighed down by particularly low forecasts by one bank which saw the index falling to 116 in the current quarter and only partly recovering to 120 over the following nine months. It did not give its reasons.
Most analysts concurred with Petersen, not a member of the panel, and with latest government data pointing to increased growth and a cut in state budget deficits.

"Against the background of good company half-year results and positive full-year expectations, as well as increased sales potential in traditional export markets, we estimate that shares have good potential," said analyst Morten Kristensen, of bank Spar Nord, the only panelist who agreed to be named.
At the top end of the prediction scale was a forecast of 129 by the end of January, 133 in six months time and a hefty 140 by next October.

Dealers said that Tuesday's KFX gains, up 0.99 point from Friday, were linked to the performance of foreign markets and were not affected by latest government forecasts of improved growth, reduced public debt and fewer unemployed.
"The forecasts are exactly as expected, there's no big news there. The optimistic view presented in the government's August forecast has since been confirmed by monthly indicators," an analyst said.
